newsitem.title: UK: Northern Ireland police escape guerrilla ambush.
newsitem.headline: Northern Ireland police escape guerrilla ambush.

text.p: Suspected Irish republican guerrillas fired a rocket-grenade at a police vehicle in Belfast, capital of British-ruled Northern Ireland, late on Thursday.
"At this stage we have no reports of injuries," a security source said.
The grenade was believed to have missed its target and hit a school wall.
The ambush occurred in a residential district in the north of the city.
"There was an attack on a police mobile patrol on Limstone Road. It looks as though something has either been fired or thrown but most likely it was fired," said the source.
First reports said the grenade appeared to have been of a type often used by Irish Republican Army (IRA) guerrillas.
No group has claimed responsibility for the attack.

British security forces, on alert for IRA attacks after two police officers were shot dead in the town of Lurgan on June 16, immediately sealed off the area. Army bomb disposal officers were called to the scene.

On Wednesday, police thwarted a planned attack by guerrillas on a police patrol in the west of the city. Security officers said the IRA, which is fighting British rule in Northern Ireland, was behind that incident.
Northern Ireland has been tense for months amid a resurgence of IRA hostilities that has triggered apparent revenge attacks by pro-British Loyalist groups.
The tension coincides with fears of trouble being sparked by a series of street parades by Protestants, who support continued rule from London. The parades reach their climax in mid-July.

The latest guerrilla incident came 36 hours after British Prime Minister Tony Blair unveiled plans aimed at getting the IRA to abandon its 28-year campaign of violence so that its Sinn Fein political wing could secure a seat at peace talks.

Blair, in a speech to parliament on Wednesday, detailed Anglo-Irish proposals for defusing a long-running dispute over how IRA weapons could be scrapped if the guerrillas called a cessation of violence.
He said full-scale talks on the province's future would start in mid-September and end next May, and that they would go ahead regardless of whether Sinn Fein was involved.
Sinn Fein says it is considering the proposals.
Britain and Ireland have consistently said the guerrillas must renounce violence before Sinn Fein can be admitted to talks.
